courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Projecting Gaussians to splats and sorting them by tile
md: The sort is per tile, by each Gaussian's center depth, not per pixel. Where two large splats interpenetrate, the true order can differ from pixel to pixel, so blending is approximate. The paper notes this error becomes negligible as splats shrink toward pixel size, and lists sudden order switches (popping) as a limitation.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: "Garbage collection solves ABA" is a common misconception that Michael calls out. GC prevents ABA caused by *reuse*, but if a program moves the same nodes back and forth between two lock-free stacks, a node can leave and return to the same position with perfect GC. Ask whether the algorithm is ABA-safe under GC first; only then do hazard pointers or epochs make it ABA-safe without GC.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Reporting an ablation people can trust
md: Report per-stage deltas with intervals, the paired test and effect size, win/loss counts, interaction cells for stages that depend on each other, and cost, all on one stated harness. A bare column of mean scores invites the wrong conclusion.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Mass assignment and property-level authorization
md: Field lists rot in one direction: new fields. A blocklist that forbids `isAdmin` today silently allows `isOwner` added next quarter. An allowlist forgets a new field by leaving it read-only, which fails safe.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM: challenge and response, and why the hash is enough
md: NTLM never sends the password, but its proof is computed only from the unsalted NT hash plus a server challenge. So the hash is the password. Move to NTLMv2 only, then to Kerberos, and watch 4776 and the 4624 package name.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: 4662 is only written if Directory Service Access auditing is on **and** the domain object's SACL asks for it. Many domains have neither, and then DCSync leaves no Security log trace at all. Check before you need it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
md: Exploitation is a ladder of capabilities: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload. Every mitigation removes or weakens one rung, and the earlier the rung, the more bug-specific and costly the attacker's workaround.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: An agent benchmark score is a property of **model + harness + environment + grader + metric**. Change any one and the number moves. Most of this course is about how each part shapes the score.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: A minimal harness: stop conditions, errors and budgets
md: Do not retry a tool blindly. Re-running a failed `git push` or a payment call can duplicate a side effect. Retry the model API transport freely, but report tool failures back to the model and let it decide, or make the tool itself idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as running it once (for example, a payment call that carries a unique request key the server uses to ignore duplicates).

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Consolidation and forgetting: reflection, decay and deletion
md: Deletion must follow lineage. Keep source pointers on every derived memory (Generative Agents already stores the cited records for each reflection) so that deleting a source can find and rewrite or delete every reflection, summary and merged fact that contains it. Also delete the embeddings and any copies in logs.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Getting data out: images, links, tool calls
md: For every LLM feature, list the ways out: rendered images, links, tools that make network requests, and the user. Close the ones you do not need and allowlist the rest. Without a way out, stolen context stays put.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
md: Poisoning is a supply chain attack on data. Verify integrity with hashes, record provenance, and treat a model from an unknown trainer like a binary from an unknown publisher.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: GNoME: active learning with DFT, and what counts as new
md: Active learning turns DFT from a verifier into a teacher: each round's results, including failures, retrain the filter, so the hit rate per DFT call keeps rising.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: APIs from zero: REST, GraphQL and what a request carries
md: An API request carries two questions: who is calling (authentication, answered by a credential in the request) and may they do this to this object (authorization, answered by the server on every request).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Retired grants (implicit and password) and client credentials
md: Modern OAuth in one line: authorization code with PKCE for anything with a user, client credentials for machine to machine, and nothing that puts tokens in URLs or passwords in clients.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
md: Misconception: "HttpOnly cookies make XSS harmless." They stop script from stealing the cookie, but injected script can still send requests through the user's browser while the page is open. Storage choices limit theft; only preventing XSS stops abuse.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
md: "No findings" does not mean "no bugs". Semgrep's own README warns that its free Community Edition analyses taint only within a single function or file, so it misses many true positives in security work. A flow that hops across files, or a source the rules do not know about, is invisible.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Vulnerability management end to end: inventory, scans, deduplication
md: Group findings by the action that fixes them and by the owner who must act. Developers do not want 300 tickets for one library upgrade; they want one ticket listing the 300 places it fixes.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
md: A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
md: Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
md: The future contract: **if `poll` returns `Pending`, the future must make sure the waker from that call gets woken later** when progress is possible. Forget it and the task hangs forever, with no error. The Tokio tutorial calls this a common source of bugs.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: What atomics cost: cache lines, contention and real uses
md: Use the most specific operation that does the job. If a fetch_add, fetch_or or swap expresses your update, prefer it to a hand-written CAS loop: it never fails, and on ARM the compiler turns it into a tight instruction sequence, which (as of Mara Bos's tests) it does not do for a hand-written CAS loop.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Who are you, prove it, and what may you do?
md: Everything in this course is for understanding and defending. Only test systems you own or have written permission to test; unauthorised access is a crime in most countries.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Account recovery: the side door around every lock
md: The account is only as secure as the easiest way to reset it. If a lost-password flow needs only an email or a phone number, those become the real password.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tokens, budgets and when to stop
md: Tokens buy research quality (80% of BrowseComp variance in Anthropic's analysis), so the budget is the main dial. Enforce budgets in the harness, reserve a share for synthesis and verification, and scale effort to the question.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: A correctly predicted branch is nearly free. A mispredicted one costs about as many cycles as the pipeline is deep. Agner Fog, whose optimization manuals measure these costs on real chips, gives roughly 0 to 2 cycles for a predicted branch and about 15 to 25 cycles for a misprediction on modern x86 cores.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool
md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
md: Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query patch outputs to predict the next byte.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: A clean Miri run is evidence, not proof. Miri is dynamic: it only checks the paths your tests execute, and the Book notes it does not cover every way code can be unsound. Combine it with tests that hit the edge cases, such as mid = len and mid = len + 1.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
md: A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stored XSS and the worms it made: Samy and TweetDeck
md: Both worms are stored XSS that spread because the payload could use the victim's session to store itself again. Both trace back to a gap in **output encoding**: a filter that guessed at browser parsing (MySpace) and one rendering path that skipped escaping (TweetDeck). Encoding has to happen on every path, as the very last step before data enters HTML.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
md: CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: How AWS decides: explicit deny, SCPs, boundaries and resource policies
md: "We added an Allow, so it should work" is the classic debugging trap. If anything anywhere has a matching `Deny`, including an SCP you cannot see from inside the account, no Allow will help. AWS's documentation advises asking your organization's administrators when an SCP might be the cause.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Incident response for a leaked cloud key
md: For a leaked key: deactivate first, then investigate with CloudTrail across all Regions, then hunt for persistence (new users, keys, roles and policies) before declaring it closed. Then remove the reason a long-lived key existed at all.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: A column in memory is a few flat buffers: values (or offsets plus data) and a validity bitmap. Flat, typed, contiguous buffers are what make tight loops and SIMD over columns possible.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops
md: Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Grounding: Set-of-Mark labels, DOM and accessibility trees
md: Misconception: Set-of-Mark always improves GUI grounding. Both SeeAct and OSWorld saw marks underperform richer text grounding on dense screens. Marks help most when there are few, well-separated elements.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan reports races that **did not cause a failure** in this run. It needs only that both conflicting accesses execute and that nothing orders them by happens-before. That is its big advantage over stress testing.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: A read that overlaps a write may return either the old or the new value. Once any read has returned the new value and completed, every later-starting read must return it too. Linearizability forbids the value from flickering back.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: Bounded loads caps *load per server*, not *load per key*. If one key alone exceeds a server's capacity, forwarding spreads its requests across servers only when any server can answer for it, as with a cache that can fetch from the origin. A database shard that alone holds the data still needs the replication or splitting tools from the previous lesson.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Arc consistency is not the same as a solution. Three variables with domain $\{1,2\}$ and pairwise $\neq$ constraints are fully arc-consistent (every value has a support on every arc), yet no assignment satisfies all three. Propagation shrinks the search; it does not replace it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Ship the least software that runs your app: multi-stage builds into a minimal or distroless base, scanned in CI and rescanned while running.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: RBAC only adds. Grant namespaced Roles with explicit resources, names and verbs. Treat Secrets list, pod creation, nodes/proxy, escalate, bind and impersonate as administrator-level rights.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: base64 hides nothing. Lock down who can get, list or watch Secrets and who can create pods, encrypt etcd data with a KMS provider, rewrite existing Secrets after enabling it, and keep high-value credentials in an external store.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Why a multi-turn search needs explicit state
md: The state object, not the transcript, is the source of truth for what the user wants right now. The LLM proposes changes to it; code applies them; the query is a pure function of it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: When to ask a clarifying question instead of guessing
md: Do not ask about what the state already answers, or about slots marked dontcare. Repeated or redundant questions are the fastest way to make mixed-initiative feel worse than a plain search box.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: CoT monitoring is most trustworthy where the CoT is necessary: behaviors that need long serial reasoning must pass through readable tokens. It is weakest for behaviors a model can do in one forward pass, and it stays useful only as long as training does not teach the CoT to look clean.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
md: Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: More stages are not automatically faster. Each stage costs shared memory that a bigger tile or an epilogue staged through shared memory could use, and once loads are hidden, extra stages add nothing. StageCountAuto simply fills what is left.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: From device to NUMA node: decoders, interleaving and regions
md: Pick the memory zone deliberately. Hot-plugged CXL memory can be onlined as `ZONE_MOVABLE` or `ZONE_NORMAL`. Kernel allocations are generally not migratable and can only use `ZONE_NORMAL` or lower, so CXL memory in `ZONE_MOVABLE` serves only user pages and other movable data. `daxctl` onlines as movable by default; that keeps kernel data off the device but means CXL capacity cannot absorb kernel memory pressure.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Vectorizing means rewriting a scalar loop, which handles one element per instruction, into SIMD instructions that handle 8 at once, and compilers can do it automatically. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
md: Determinism leaks are easy to write. Reading the real clock, spawning an OS thread, seeding from OS entropy, or iterating a hash map whose order is randomized per process (Rust's default `HashMap` is) all make the same seed produce different runs. FoundationDB avoids multithreaded concurrency entirely and deploys one node per core instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
md: Anything a privileged job reads (a cache, an artifact, a downloaded tool, a config file) is part of its input. Ask who could have written it. If the answer includes a fork, a PR or a comment, the privileged job must treat it as untrusted data or not read it at all.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency). Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
md: The weight $\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$ is what makes DPO work. The authors report that a naive version without this weighting (push chosen up, rejected down, equally on every pair) can make the language model degenerate.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it
md: Two independent writes have no shared order and no shared atomicity. Either keep one store authoritative and repair the other, or derive the second store from the first store's commit log.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: The verifier is a **safety** check, not a security review. It proves your program cannot crash or hang the kernel; it does not judge what the program observes. That is why loading tracing programs requires root, or both the CAP_BPF and CAP_PERFMON capabilities (slices of root's privilege granted on their own: CAP_BPF for loading BPF programs and maps, CAP_PERFMON for tracing).

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Order of operations for edge models: pick an efficient architecture and distill into it, quantize to int8 with per-channel weights, fall back to QAT if accuracy drops, prune only when your runtime benefits, and verify accuracy, latency and peak RAM on the actual device.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Why raw strings break filters and joins
md: Normalize to an ID, filter on the ID, and keep the raw string for display and debugging. Run the **same** normalizer on queries and on profiles, or the two sides drift apart and matches silently disappear.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
md: Attention in serving is mostly about **memory traffic under irregular shapes**. FlashInfer's answer is to separate what is static (variant, layout, tile sizes: compile time) from what is dynamic (lengths, page lists: a cheap per-step plan).

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
md: Testing samples behaviors; verification covers all of them. Model checking covers every behavior of a bounded model of the design. Proof covers every behavior of the code, but only for the properties you wrote down.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: Do not copy FP16's overflow handling. FP16 automatic mixed precision (PyTorch's autocast with a dynamic loss scaler) skips the update and shrinks the loss scale when an overflow appears. The FP8 paper explains that overflows are much more likely in FP8's narrow range, so skipping would discard too many steps; FP8 recipes **saturate** out-of-range values to the maximum instead.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
md: `synchronous_commit = off` and `fsync = off` sound similar but are not. The first may lose the last ~600 ms (by default) of acknowledged commits and stays consistent. The second can corrupt the whole cluster (PostgreSQL's word for all the databases one server manages) and is only for data you can recreate, such as an initial bulk load.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Measuring fuzzers honestly: coverage, crashes and statistics
md: "Unique crashes" is not a bug count. When a tool, a vendor pitch or your own dashboard reports it, ask how deduplication was done and how many distinct fixes the crashes needed.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
md: Verified so far: AI agents can find real bugs by variant analysis (Big Sleep, SQLite), AI-written harnesses extend fuzzing coverage and find real CVEs (OSS-Fuzz, OpenSSL), and attackers use AI to find logic flaws (GTIG 2026). In every defensive case, a concrete reproducer and a sanitizer or test confirmed the bug.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head (the final prediction layers) fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or calling s0.wait_stream(s1) before the free, which makes all later work on s0 wait for the work already queued on s1) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling (storing values that do not fit in registers out in slower memory). Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
md: Do not estimate GraphRAG cost from the number of documents alone. Cost scales with total tokens, chunk size, gleaning rounds, the number of entities and relationships that need summaries, and the number of communities. The official docs open with a warning that GraphRAG can consume a lot of LLM resources and suggest starting small.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: The split in R1 is telling: verifiable rewards where answers can be checked (math, code, logic), learned reward models only where they cannot, and those kept short because they get hacked.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: A higher IPC is not automatically better. A thread spinning on a lock retires instructions quickly, so it shows high IPC while making no logical progress. Judge IPC together with the instruction count and the run time.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Mitigations, their costs, and checking a real machine
md: `mitigations=off` is sometimes recommended in benchmark blogs. On any machine that runs code you do not fully trust (a browser, CI jobs, containers from others, VMs of other tenants), that trades a few percent of speed for letting that code read memory it should not. Measure your workload first; most of the cost is concentrated in system-call-heavy paths.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: The synchronous stall is the classic THP latency spike. `/proc/vmstat` counts it: `compact_stall` increments every time a process stalls to run compaction, with `compact_success` and `compact_fail` alongside. A rising `compact_stall` next to tail-latency spikes is a strong hint. Tail latency is the time of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile, called p99.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on Musique the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
md: Use HyDE where its strength is real: no labels, a weak or unsupervised encoder, domain or format shift, and a latency budget of seconds. Keep the query in the average, cap passage length, sample in parallel, and route by query type. The paper itself suggests serving HyDE early, then shifting traffic to a supervised retriever as logs grow, keeping HyDE for rare and emerging queries.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Ask two questions of any industrial protocol: does the receiver verify who sent this command, and can it tell if the command was changed or replayed? For classic Modbus and plain DNP3 the answer is no, so the network around them must do that job.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: In OT incident response, first make the process safe (using instruments you trust), then keep it running by hand if needed, and only then contain, investigate and restore from offline backups.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: A robust change detector is: align (features, RANSAC, homography, optional ECC refinement), mask invalid warped borders, correct photometry using pixels that probably did not change, difference, threshold (Otsu when the histogram is two-humped), then open the mask with a kernel smaller than the smallest change you care about.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
md: Hash at collection, hash at every transfer, analyse only copies. A hash that matches the one recorded at acquisition is what lets you say "this is exactly what we took from the machine".

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: When the incident is not an attack: CrowdStrike, July 2024
md: Treat large non-malicious outages with the same machinery as attacks: incident commander, severity, OOB communications, a timeline and a blameless review. Attackers will use the confusion either way.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Shellshock: when an environment variable became code
md: Shellshock is injection into an interpreter nobody thought was in the path. The data (a header) was never concatenated into code by the application; the interpreter itself treated a data channel (the environment) as code. Know which interpreters your input reaches, including the ones your libraries start for you.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
md: Every production allocator is the same four layers: size classes, a lock-free local cache, a shared per-size-class middle, and a page-level back-end that talks to the OS. The interesting differences are *who owns the local cache* (thread, CPU, or page), *how objects freed by another thread get home*, and *when idle pages go back to the OS*.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy
md: For language models, decide two things: what sequences you train on (references, teacher outputs, or the student's own samples) and which divergence you minimize (forward KL covers all modes, reverse KL picks one). On-policy training fixes the train-inference mismatch.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: `chmod 777` is not a fix for "permission denied". It lets every account on the machine, including a compromised web server account, modify the file. If a script run by root is world-writable, any user can make root run their code. Find the account that actually needs access and grant only that.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
md: A signal handler can interrupt any line of code, so it must only do async-signal-safe work, and a fix must be guarded by a test or it can quietly disappear in a refactor, as this one did after 14 years.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
md: For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
md: OWASP's top LLM risk guidance says it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention of prompt injection exists, and recommends treating the model as an untrusted user. Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do much damage: least-privilege tools (each tool gets only the permissions its job needs), human approval for high-risk actions, and checks outside the model.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
md: Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
md: Constrained decoding does not make the model understand the format. It removes the illegal choices at each step and lets the model choose among what is left. An FSM state tells you which tokens are legal; a precomputed index makes that lookup cheap.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
md: Errors are not equal. A **spurious** filter (q6's remote_ok, q7's required javascript) removes good results and the user never sees them. A **missing** filter only returns extra results the user can see and skip. Track precision and recall of slots separately and weight spurious filters as the worse error.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
md: Write the cost model before choosing the method: calls on the critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model size. Then check quality on your own queries: the cheapest design that holds your NDCG@10 wins.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
md: Routing failures are silent. A wrong answer from the weak model looks like any other answer, and the dashboard shows only that costs went down. Log the routed model with every response (Bedrock returns it), and compare quality by route, not just overall.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
md: A homography is only correct for planar scenes or pure camera rotation. For a general 3D scene seen from two positions, matches satisfy a fundamental or essential matrix instead, and forcing a homography will reject many correct matches.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: EBR is fast because readers only write their own epoch when they pin, but it is not strictly lock-free for memory: Fraser notes that a process that stalls inside a critical region stops the limbo lists (Fraser's name for the per-epoch garbage bags) from ever being reclaimed. Hazard pointers bound the unreclaimed memory (at most NR nodes) at the cost of publishing and re-validating every pointer before use.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
md: The whole course in one line: a log template is the cheapest useful abstraction over log text, and the only one that turns an unbounded stream of unique strings into a small set of countable events. Everything after it, counting, baselining, sequence models, dashboards, inherits both its power and its errors.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
md: A converted query is only as right as its pipeline's field mapping. If your SIEM stores Sysmon in a different source, or the 4688 field is NewProcessName rather than Image, the query is valid, runs, and silently matches nothing. Always test converted rules against real events from your own environment.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Position Interpolation and NTK-aware scaling
md: Uniform interpolation protects the slow pairs but blurs the fast ones. Every better method since PI is about treating pairs differently according to their wavelength.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: Looping saves **parameters** (memory, communication), not **compute**. Every loop is another full pass through the block, and the passes are sequential, so a $(1 \otimes 12)$ model is about as slow per token as a 12-layer model. Looped models trade memory for depth, they do not make inference free.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: Why full fine-tuning is expensive, and why it may not need to be
md: A d90 of 200 does not mean that 200 hand-picked weights would do. The 200 numbers are projected through a dense random map, so every original weight still moves a little. And 90% of full performance is the bar, not 100%.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" (or its perplexity, $e$ to the average per-token loss, as in the prerequisite course) is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The malware economy: loaders, access brokers and RaaS
md: Ransomware is the last step of a chain, not the first. Loader infections, sold remote-access logins and hands-on intrusion usually come days or weeks before encryption, which is your window to detect and evict.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Command and control: beacons, jitter and Cobalt Strike
md: Regular is not the same as malicious. Software updaters, mail clients, telemetry and monitoring agents all beacon. Use regularity to rank what to review, then check the destination (age of domain, reputation, who else talks to it) and the process that made the connections (Sysmon event 3).

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention, Dao et al. 2022, which computes attention tile by tile in fast on-chip memory; also in NVIDIA's Transformer Engine library) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Use-after-free and double free: dangling pointers
md: Chromium reports that about 70 percent of its high-severity security bugs are memory safety problems, and that half of those are use-after-free. Lifetimes are the hardest promise to keep by hand in a large C++ program.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Unmerged does not mean easy. Requests in one batch use adapters with different ranks and different sequence lengths, so padding everything into one batched matmul wastes work. S-LoRA's variant that copies adapters into contiguous memory and uses padded batched matmul (S-LoRA-bmm) was much slower than the version with custom kernels, GPU functions written for exactly this mixed-rank job.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Union versus RRF, and deduplicating by document id
md: RRF rewards agreement between phrasings. A relevant document that only one phrasing finds stays low, and a junk document that two phrasings share can outrank it. That is why the quality of the phrasings matters as much as their number.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Common misconception: an MTP model does not have to emit several tokens per step. Gloeckle et al. use only the next-token head for ordinary decoding. The other heads are optional, and lesson 5 shows how they can be reused to draft tokens for faster decoding.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
md: A frequent mistake is to read $L^{-1/4}$ as an elementwise power. It is a *matrix* power: eigendecompose $L = Q \Lambda Q^\top$ and take $Q \Lambda^{-1/4} Q^\top$. That needs float32 (or better) and an eigensolver, which is why roots are only refreshed every $f$ steps.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Common misconception: "SP is broken only because the learning rate is too large for big models." Lowering it uniformly fixes the exploding layers but freezes others, such as the input embeddings. The issue is the *relative* scaling between layers.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed is not a weaker form of a single consistent view. Each statement sees one snapshot, but an updating statement can also see newer versions of the rows it is about to change, so a single UPDATE or DELETE can mix two moments in time. The docs call it unsuitable for commands with complex search conditions.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
md: The repair rule is not cosmetic: it changes your score. [seqeval](https://github.com/chakki-works/seqeval) documents that for gold `B-NP I-NP O` and prediction `I-NP I-NP O`, its default mode (which mimics the conlleval Perl script) gives precision, recall and F1 of 1.00, while `mode='strict'` with `scheme=IOB2` gives 0.00. Same predictions, two different papers' worth of difference. Always say which mode you used.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
md: Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the KV cache. NSA adds compressed and per-branch keys; DSA adds an indexer key per token. Both cut the bytes *read and computed* per query. Also, DSA's indexer is still $O(L^2)$ over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: The single controller does not mean all tensors flow through one process. Large transfers, especially weight refit, go over channels the controller sets up (CUDA IPC or NCCL), not through the controller itself. A CUDA IPC (inter-process communication) handle is a small token that lets another process on the same machine open the same GPU memory without copying it.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RPKI and route origin validation
md: RPKI answers 'may this AS originate this prefix?'. It turns the most common hijack, a wrong origin or an unexpected more specific, into an Invalid route that validating networks drop. It does not validate paths or stop leaks with the correct origin.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Layers: the OSI and TCP/IP models, and why both exist
md: Models are maps, not territory. Real protocols do not always fit one layer: ARP (lesson 5) sits between layers 2 and 3, and TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption under HTTPS; lesson 12) between 4 and 7. Use the numbers to communicate, not to argue about where a protocol "really" belongs.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Proxies, VPNs and firewalls
md: A VPN is not anonymity and a firewall is not a security boundary for everything. The VPN provider sees what your ISP used to see, and a firewall that allows port 443 allows every attack that arrives over port 443. Each control answers one question; know which one.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Simplified model: it ignores caches, assumes perfect overlap, symmetric links and that threads can saturate their controller. Real numbers differ by machine, so measure with your workload. The *ordering* of the options is what the model teaches.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Where candidate boxes come from: proposals, anchors and grids
md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
md: "We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker
md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by

lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
